rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, two-year (2017-2018) field experiment in a gray jujube orchard, Qiemo County, Xinjiang, 12 plots, 3 micro-sprinkler levels plus control. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 4, soluble sugar increased 2.7-6.5% in 2017 and 2-4.3% in 2018 under micro-sprinkler treatments; yield of T2 and T3 significantly higher in 2017, T2 highest each year at 6687 kg/hm2 (2017) and 6748 kg/hm2 (2018). Q4: Sections 3.1-3.2, 4.3 and Figs. 3-6, the authors measured air temperature, relative humidity, derived VPD, and leaf Pn/Tr/Gs, and regressed yield and soluble sugar against leaf Pn (Fig. 6), linking the sprinkler-induced VPD reduction to photosynthesis and then to yield and sugar. Q8: Section 4.3 end, the authors state that yield and soluble sugar appear to increase with reduced VPD even though many other factors are known to affect such relations, that VPD alone may not explain all aspects of stress and is only a null model, and that leaf gas exchange was measured over a single day per year and not intended for carbon balance.
rows.notes: The technology field says drip but the passage explicitly names micro-sprinkler irrigation; the study tests micro-sprinkler cooling applied on top of a uniform drip system in all plots, so its own result matches the passage's technology. Q3: single method (hand harvest and lab assays), no independent second method. Q5/Q6: one site, one crop, 500 m2 plots. Q7: the authors note the effect was strongest at 4 mm/d at the flowering-fruit set stage and recommend arid/semi-arid regions, but do not state these as required conditions. Q9: Table 4 gives treatment means with letter groupings only, no SD/SE/CI for yield or sugar.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, two-year field experiment on gray jujube with four treatments in randomized plots. Q2: Section 3.1 and Tables 1-3, micro-sprinkler treatments lowered mean air temperature by 2.3-3.2 C (2017) and 1.2-2.1 C (2018) relative to control and raised relative humidity by about 11-17%; Section 4.3 and Fig. 3, VPD computed from measured Ta and RH declined consistently from control to T2 (roughly 3 to 2 kPa per abstract; Table 5 own research row reports VPD down 0.53-0.54 kPa). Q4: Tables 1-3 and Eq. 2, the authors measured air temperature and relative humidity at four heights and before/during/after events, the two variables through which spraying reduces VPD, and computed VPD from them. Q9: Fig. 3 caption, VPD values (and Pn, Tr, Gs) are reported as mean plus/minus SE of three replicates.
rows.notes: Technology field says drip but passage names micro-sprinkler irrigation, which is what the study tests (drip was uniform background irrigation in all plots). Q3: single method (temperature-humidity sensors; VPD derived from the same readings). Q5/Q6: single site, crop and climate; plot scale only. Q7: the cooling effect was found to be concentrated in the lower canopy (0-100 cm) and larger with greater spray amounts, but no condition is stated as a requirement. Q8: the stated limitations concern the one-day leaf gas exchange measurements and VPD as a null model, not the micro-climate result itself; the non-significance at 200 cm is reported as a result rather than a limitation.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Figures 2-6 are described by captions only. The study combines micro-sprinkler cooling with background drip irrigation; the review labels the technology as drip, but the cited passage is about micro-sprinkler irrigation, which is the treatment variable in the study.
